h1: Whisky with a splash of coconut water and other Indian mixers
title: Whisky with Coconut Water and Mixers | Craft Beer School
desc: How to mix whisky with coconut water, nimbu soda, ginger ale and other Indian mixers: which whisky, what ratio and how to keep it fresh.
teaser: Whisky and coconut water is a coastal classic. Here is how to get it right, along with other Indian mixers.
standfirst: Indian drinkers have always mixed whisky with what was cold, local and refreshing. Coconut water, nimbu soda and ginger each suit a different whisky. The ratio matters more than the brand.
sections: Mixing whisky is not a crime

A lot of whisky snobbery is about drinking it neat. In a hot country, that advice makes less sense. A long, cold drink with a mixer spreads one measure over a tall glass, keeps you hydrated and suits a slow evening. Indian drinkers worked this out long ago.

The trick is to pick a whisky that suits the mixer and to get the ratio right. Most mixed drinks fail because they are too strong or use a whisky that fights the mixer.

Coconut water is sweet, slightly nutty and lightly salty. It is common as a mixer in coastal regions such as Kerala and Goa, where tender coconuts are everywhere. It softens whisky and adds a gentle sweetness without the sugar load of cola.

Choose a light or fruity whisky: a smooth blend, a grain whisky or a light single malt matured in ex-bourbon casks. Heavily peated or sherry cask whiskies tend to clash with the delicate coconut flavour.

Start with about 30 ml of whisky to 120 to 150 ml of chilled coconut water, over ice. Fresh tender coconut water tastes much better than packaged. It also spoils quickly once opened, so use it within hours and keep it cold.
Nimbu soda and the fresh lime family

Fresh lime soda, sweet, salted or mixed, is one of India's great drinks on its own. With whisky it becomes a sharp, refreshing long drink. Squeeze half a lime into a tall glass, add 30 ml of whisky, a pinch of salt or sugar to taste, then ice and chilled soda.

A light blend or a lightly peated whisky both work here. Lime brightens fruit and cuts through any heaviness. A pinch of kala namak, black salt, adds a savoury edge that some drinkers love.
Ginger suits spice, cola hides everything

• Ginger ale or ginger beer: a natural partner for spicy whiskies, rye and bourbon. Add a lime wedge.
  • Cola: very sweet, so it hides most of the whisky. Use an inexpensive blend and go light on the measure.
  • Plain soda: the classic highball, best for showing the whisky itself.
  • Chilled water: the simplest mixer of all and still the best for tasting.

Our guide to adding water to whisky explains why even a small splash changes the aroma.

For a long drink, one part whisky to three or four parts mixer is a good starting point. That brings a 40% ABV whisky down to roughly 8 to 10% ABV in the glass, closer to strong beer or wine than to a neat pour.

Measure the whisky with a jigger rather than pouring freely. Generous home pours are how a relaxed evening turns into a heavy one. Keep the mixer well chilled so the ice melts slowly and the drink stays balanced.
A tired mixer ruins a good whisky

Use a tall glass filled with ice. More ice keeps a drink colder for longer because it melts more slowly than a few cubes in a warm glass. Make ice from clean, filtered water; tap water ice can carry chlorine or other off flavours into the drink.

Mixers go flat or stale quickly once opened in Indian heat. Buy soda in small bottles, keep coconut water cold and use fresh limes. A tired mixer ruins a good whisky faster than any other mistake.
Regional sherbets make good mixers too

Coconut water and nimbu soda are the best known, but there are other local mixers worth trying. Kokum sherbet, tangy and deep red, is popular along the Konkan coast and pairs well with a light blend over ice. Aam panna, made from raw mango, adds sourness and a little salt. Jaljeera, the cumin and mint drink, brings a savoury, spiced edge that suits a peppery whisky.

These mixers are often sweetened, so taste them first and adjust the ratio. A sweet sherbet may need more soda to keep the drink from turning syrupy. Go light on the whisky with strongly flavoured mixers. They will hide much of what the whisky brings.

Pour three small measures of the same light whisky, about 15 ml each. Mix one with chilled coconut water, one with fresh lime soda and one with plain soda, each at roughly one to four. Taste them side by side and note what each mixer brings out or hides.

Have soft versions of each drink ready for anyone not drinking. Coconut water and nimbu soda are excellent on their own. Pace yourself, drink water and nobody who has been drinking drives. That simple test will tell you which mixer suits your whisky and your evening.
faqs: Can you mix whisky with coconut water?
Yes. A light or fruity whisky with chilled fresh coconut water, about one part to four or five, makes a soft, refreshing long drink.
What is the best ratio for whisky and a mixer?
One part whisky to three or four parts mixer is a good starting point for a long drink.
Which whisky is best with mixers?
A smooth blend, grain whisky or light single malt suits most mixers. Save complex, expensive whiskies for drinking neat or with water.
No. Mixing changes how it tastes but suits hot weather well. Choose a whisky that matches the mixer.
